speaker: Dr Charlene Chen
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what measures are in place to proactively detect and prevent the misuse of SkillsFuture credits, especially by operators using multi-level marketing tactics or exploiting the credit expiry timeline; and (b) how does the Ministry ensure training quality and learner protection against the marketing tactics by such operators.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what steps are the Ministry and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) taking to pro-actively monitor and enforce compliance with marketing requirements and practice guidelines by training providers to better protect all learners, including low-income and older workers; and (b) whether the Ministry would consider mandating public disclosure of provider-level data, such as drop-out rates and course-to-job conversions, to strengthen these safeguards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: For example, SSG has reminded training providers to focus on promoting the merits of the courses, and not use the expiry of the SkillsFuture Credits to hard-sell their courses to individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Given the large number of training providers, SSG supplements its own monitoring of their marketing behaviour by relying on feedback and whistle-blowing by the general public and learners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: The majority of our training providers comply with SSG's marketing guidelines, and the practice of engaging third parties for direct marketing is not widespread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Nevertheless, SSG has taken action to address public feedback to avoid such undesirable practices from proliferating, which could bring the training sector into disrepute and harm the interests of learners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Publishing performance data of training providers is another safeguard for learners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: SSG requires learners taking SSG-funded programmes to give feedback on course quality and how well the training supports their career growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Safeguarding public trust and confidence in our lifelong learning system is a key priority for SSG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: We will continue to monitor training providers' marketing behaviour, adjust our guidelines and take fair and proportionate enforcement actions where necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: We remind our training providers to abide strictly by the marketing guidelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Education)
text: We also seek continued support from the public, to be vigilant and to provide feedback on non-compliant marketing practices.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Janil, I assume your reply is also in response to Oral Question No 17?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Yes, please, if you do not mind, I would like to address oral Question Nos 16 and 17 together.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Many Singaporeans, including our residents in Tampines, are anxious about employability.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Skills upgrading must be built on trust to protect our learners and we need to ensure that training providers are credible, relevant courses are provided and public funds are used responsibly.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Number one, what avenues are available for whistle-blowers, especially those who are not digitally-savvy to report unethical course practises?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And number two, if participants find that courses fall short of the promised content, what recourse or mechanisms are there?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And lastly, will there be regular audits besides relying on feedback from course participants?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Not all of them are online and digital, and we do engage directly with training providers to make sure that they also are looking for feedback, as well as the institutions that are curating the courses.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the feedback can be about the service provider as a whole – the faculty, for example, or the course.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have several lines of communication to make sure that we do receive feedback.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The recourse will depend very much on what the nature of the complaint is.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not always possible to get a refund, if that is what Dr Chen is asking about.
